title: India's 'own GPS', which new ISRO satellite can restore
syllabus: GS3 › Awareness in the field of space; Indigenisation of technology and developing new technology; Security challenges and their management in border areas · GS4 › Foundational values: courage of conviction, fortitude
summary: ISRO is launching NVS-03 to restore NavIC, India's regional navigation system, which stopped giving location data after repeated satellite failures.
ideas: Strategic sovereignty in space: NavIC (the working name of IRNSS) is a seven-satellite system covering India and up to 1,500 km around it. India is the only country with a regional navigation system; the four global ones are GPS, GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou.
GS3 · Space / strategic autonomy
NavIC gives India its own positioning, navigation and timing, so it need not depend on foreign systems such as GPS in a crisis.

Serving citizens and soldiers: when fully working, NavIC gives the public accuracy of up to 10 metres and a restricted, fee-based service to users such as the military. It covers the Indian landmass better than GPS, whose signals reach India at an angle and struggle in valleys and forests.
GS3 · Dual-use technology / border security
As a dual-use system, NavIC serves both public navigation and the armed forces, with better coverage in India's valleys and forests than GPS.

Imported parts were the weak link: six of the 11 navigation satellites launched since 2013 failed, mainly because of defective imported atomic clocks. Replacements also failed: IRNSS-1H's heat shield did not open and NVS-02's propulsion failed. The Centre told Parliament this year that the system no longer gave position data.
GS3 · Indigenisation / critical components
NavIC's failures show that a strategic system is only as sovereign as its least indigenous component.

Learning from failure: from NVS-01, satellites carry Indian-made atomic clocks with a 12-year life (up from 10), and propulsion systems now get more thorough checks. The new L1 frequency, the band GPS mostly uses, lets NavIC work with other systems and run on low-power chips in smartwatches.
GS3 · Indigenisation · GS4 · Learning organisation
By building its own atomic clocks and tightening checks after failures, ISRO turned setbacks into a stronger second generation of NavIC.
keywords: The three services a navigation system gives
Strategic autonomy in PNT is as vital as autonomy in energy or defence.
Reliance on imports for parts a system cannot work without
Critical component dependence, as with NavIC's imported atomic clocks, can ground an entire strategic system.
Ability to work alongside other systems
Adding the L1 band makes NavIC interoperable with GPS and usable in everyday devices.
Technology serving both civilian and military needs
NavIC is dual-use: a public utility in peace and a strategic asset in conflict.
Risk of a foreign system being switched off or degraded in a crisis
An indigenous system guards against signal denial during conflict.
Coverage limited to a region rather than the whole world
India chose a regional system, giving it focused coverage at a fraction of a global constellation's cost.
examples: Defective imported clocks caused most of NavIC's satellite failures
NavIC's imported atomic clocks failing is a textbook case of strategic risk from critical imports.
New-generation satellites add the L1 band used by low-power wearable chips
With the L1 band, NavIC reaches everyday devices such as smartwatches.
After clock, heat-shield and propulsion failures, ISRO built clocks at home, tightened checks and launched again
ISRO's return to launch after repeated failures shows institutional courage: owning mistakes and persisting.
pyqs: The advantage India saw in IRNSS: an independent regional system; the NavIC setbacks test that promise.
Why India needs IRNSS: sovereignty, better coverage of the Indian landmass, security.
Space applications for socio-economic development: navigation for transport, fisheries, disaster management.

trend.t: UPSC first asked about navigation directly: the advantage of IRNSS over GPS (GS3 2015) and why India needs IRNSS (GS1 2018). Later space questions moved to specific missions: a space station (2019), Chandrayaan-3 (2023) and Mission Drishti (2026).
trend.watch: IRNSS has been asked twice, in two different papers (GS3 2015, GS1 2018). Navigation is a must-study area, now with the failures and the indigenous fix.
focus: Need for and advantages of NavIC over GPS
Civil and military uses of NavIC
Recent ISRO missions and their objectives

potential: NavIC's setbacks highlight the risks of dependence on imported critical components in strategic technologies. Discuss, and suggest measures to strengthen India's space-based navigation capability. (15 marks)
Why does India need its own regional navigation system when global systems such as GPS are freely available? Explain. (10 marks)
What changes have been made in the second generation of NavIC satellites, and how do they improve the system's usefulness? (10 marks)

practice.q: Why does India need its own regional navigation system when global systems such as GPS are freely available? Explain.

answer.t: NavIC, the seven-satellite Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System, makes India the only country with its own regional navigation system.

pts.t: Foreign systems can be switched off or degraded in a conflict; an indigenous system removes this signal-denial risk.
A restricted, encrypted service supports the armed forces in guidance, troop movement and border surveillance.
pts.ex: NavIC's fee-based restricted service for select users.

pts.t: GPS signals reach India at an angle and weaken in valleys and forests; NavIC is designed for the Indian landmass.
pts.ex: Accuracy up to 10 metres for public use.

pts.t: Precise positioning helps rescue operations and guides fishermen at sea.
Transport, logistics, surveying and large construction projects need reliable positioning.
Building satellites and indigenous atomic clocks strengthens India's space industry.
pts.ex: Indian-made atomic clocks from NVS-01 onwards.

pts.t: Learn from the imported clock failures; build key components at home.
Plan replacements ahead of satellites' end of life.
Encourage NavIC-enabled chips in phones and wearables through the L1 band.

answer.t: A fully restored NavIC would turn India's space capability into everyday strategic security.

title: The geography & economy of Punjab's long drug crisis
syllabus: GS3 › Linkages of organised crime with terrorism; Security challenges in border areas; Role of external state and non-state actors · GS2 › Issues relating to health; Government policies and interventions · GS1 › Social issues: youth, women · GS4 › Probity in governance
summary: An anti-drug activist's killing and a recent overdose death have put Punjab's 15-year drug crisis back at the centre of politics ahead of next year's Assembly elections.
ideas: Geography makes Punjab vulnerable: its 553-km border with Pakistan lies on the route from the Golden Crescent (Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran). Police officers call Pakistan's pushing of drugs into Punjab after militancy faded 'narco-terrorism'.
GS3 · Border security / narco-terrorism
Punjab's 553-km border with Pakistan places it on the Golden Crescent route, turning drug trafficking into a security threat.

Supply from all directions: heroin (chitta) comes across the border, opium and poppy husk from Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh (where cultivation is legal for medical use), charas from Himachal Pradesh, and pharmaceutical drugs from manufacturing hubs in neighbouring states.
GS3 · Organised crime · GS2 · Centre-state coordination
Drugs reach Punjab from across the border and from neighbouring states, so the fight needs coordination among states, not only border policing.

The problem shifts when pressed: as border enforcement improved, abuse of pharmaceutical drugs rose sharply, and smugglers turned to drones, mostly small Chinese quadcopters dropping heroin and arms, often in daylight.
GS3 · Technology and security
Each crackdown has shifted the trade to a new route, from heroin to pharma drugs and from land to drones.

Social and economic roots: opium had social acceptance even before Independence; a single run as a drug mule can earn about a lakh where jobs lag aspirations; easy, underhand wealth is increasingly accepted; whole families, including women, are drawn in.
GS1 · Youth / women · GS3 · Unemployment
Unemployment and social acceptance of easy money feed both addiction and the trade, making it a social as much as a security problem.

Enforcement first, prevention later: governments have followed the EDP model (Enforcement, De-addiction, Prevention), from a 'war on drugs' (2014) and supply crackdowns (2022) to Yudh Nasheyan Virudh (2025), which targeted drug money and moved to community action with 1.5 lakh village volunteers. Drugs remain available; observers say prevention and rehabilitation should come first.
GS2 · Government interventions / health
Enforcement alone has not ended Punjab's drug crisis; prevention and rehabilitation must lead, with enforcement in support.
keywords: Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran: one of the world's three major heroin-processing hubs
Punjab's western border sits on the Golden Crescent route, making it India's frontline against heroin.
Myanmar, Thailand and Laos: the other major heroin-producing region near India
India lies between the Golden Crescent in the west and the Golden Triangle in the east.
Using drugs to weaken a state or fund terror
Drug trafficking across Punjab's border is a form of narco-terrorism, not just crime.
Pressing one supply route pushes the trade to another
The shift from border heroin to pharma drugs shows the balloon effect of supply-only enforcement.
Medicines leaking from legal supply into addiction
Diversion of pharmaceutical drugs calls for tighter regulation of manufacturers and chemists.
Policing the trade versus reducing the need for drugs
A lasting answer must balance supply-side policing with demand-side prevention and rehabilitation.
Following the money hurts trafficking networks more than arresting carriers.
Involving local people in enforcement and prevention
Village volunteers make the anti-drug effort a community movement, not just a police drive.
data: Cases of drug possession for trafficking in Punjab in 2024, the highest in India (Uttar Pradesh next with 3,219)
Punjab recorded 6,060 drug-trafficking possession cases in 2024, the highest in India (NCRB).
Share of India's pharmaceutical drug seizures / heroin seizures in Punjab alone, 2024
Punjab alone accounted for about 57% of India's pharma drug seizures and 44% of heroin seizures in 2024.
Drone drops recorded by the BSF, 2021 to 2025
Drone drops on the Punjab border rose from 3 in 2021 to over 200 in 2025 (BSF).
Rise in arrests of women under the NDPS Act, 2015 to 2022
Arrests of women under the NDPS Act in Punjab rose 85% between 2015 and 2022.
Extension of BSF jurisdiction inland in Punjab, 2021
In 2021 the Centre extended the BSF's jurisdiction from 15 km to 50 km inland.
examples: The BSF set up an anti-drone intelligence wing and Punjab Police bought anti-drone guns, yet smugglers still evade them
Despite anti-drone units, drones still ferry drugs and arms across the Punjab border.
A Punjab Police DSP arrested in a multimillion-rupee drug racket, convicted in 2019
The Bhola case exposes the nexus of traffickers, police and politicians that sustains the drug trade.
Traffickers use women because they are less likely to be searched; some women addicts turn peddlers
Traffickers exploit women as carriers, adding a gender dimension to the drug trade.
Community-driven phase of Punjab's anti-drug campaign
Punjab's 1.5 lakh village volunteers show community participation as part of the fight against drugs.
pyqs: The Golden Crescent next door and the links between drugs, arms and money: the Punjab border is the live case.
Drones ferrying arms and drugs: drone drops rose from 3 (2021) to over 200 (2025).
Narco-terrorism: Pakistan pushing drugs into Punjab after militancy faded.

trend.t: UPSC moved from the links between drug trafficking and other crimes (2018) to the technology that carries drugs, drones (2023), and then to narco-terrorism as a national threat (2024). GS4 also set a case study on a frontier district overrun by narcotics (2019).
trend.watch: Drugs and security have come in GS3 in 2018, 2023 and 2024, and in a GS4 case study in 2019. Narco-terrorism is a must-study area.
focus: Narco-terrorism and the Golden Crescent and Golden Triangle
Drones and technology in border smuggling
Supply-side vs demand-side strategy; de-addiction and rehabilitation

potential: Punjab's drug crisis is as much a socio-economic problem as a security challenge. Critically examine, and suggest a balanced strategy combining enforcement, de-addiction and prevention. (15 marks)
Tighter border enforcement has shifted the drug trade to pharmaceutical drugs and drones. Discuss the challenges this poses and the measures needed. (10 marks)
India lies between the Golden Crescent and the Golden Triangle. Examine the implications for its internal security. (10 marks)

practice.q: Tighter border enforcement has shifted the drug trade to pharmaceutical drugs and drones. Discuss the challenges this poses and the measures needed.
parts: Introduction: the shift in one line, with facts

answer.t: Punjab accounted for about 57% of India's pharma drug seizures in 2024, and BSF-recorded drone drops rose from 3 in 2021 to over 200 in 2025.

pts.t: Pressure on one route pushes the trade to another, so supply-only enforcement keeps chasing the problem.
pts.ex: Heroin to pharma drugs after border tightening.

pts.t: Pharma drugs come from licensed manufacturers and chemists, making them harder to police than contraband.
pts.ex: About 80% enter Punjab from hubs in neighbouring states.

pts.t: Supply comes from several states, but policing is state-wise, leaving coordination gaps.
Small quadcopters drop drugs and arms, often in daylight, and evade detection.
The same drones carry arms, tying drug smuggling to terrorism.
Collusion between traffickers, police and politicians weakens enforcement.
Track sales of habit-forming medicines from manufacturer to chemist.
Layered detection and jamming along the border, with BSF–state police coordination.
Financial investigation to break trafficking networks.
De-addiction, rehabilitation and jobs for youth, with community participation.

answer.t: Only a strategy that cuts both supply and demand can break a trade that adapts faster than enforcement.

title: 'Can take on grenade, what about idle youths?': Punjab Police despair in border areas
where: Front page anchor, continued on page 2 (Man Aman Singh Chhina)
syllabus: GS3 › Linkages between organised crime and terrorism; Role of external state and non-state actors; Security challenges in border areas · GS2 › India and its neighbourhood; Indian diaspora · GS1 › Youth and unemployment · GS4 › Probity, courage
summary: In Punjab's border districts, gangs with handlers abroad have killed policemen and sarpanchs this year; officers say idle youth drawn to gangs is the deeper problem. (Linked to today's card on Punjab's drug crisis.)
ideas: Crime, terror and handlers abroad: 10–15 gangs operate in Punjab with leaders abroad, in extortion and drugs, reportedly backed by Pakistan's ISI; gangs post videos claiming killings, and an ISI-linked outfit keeps surfacing.
GS3 · Organised crime–terror nexus
Punjab's gangs fuse extortion, drugs and cross-border backing, a textbook crime–terror nexus.

Local officials as targets: since February, six attacks on police personnel have killed five, and sarpanchs and their relatives are being killed; exposed posts, some without boundary walls, show a thinly protected front line.
GS3 · Border area policing
Attacks on police posts and village heads show how border-area governance itself has become a target.
Idle youth, the deeper problem: officers say it is a socio-economic challenge, as young people seek 'work' from gangs, gangsters build social media followings, and quick bail weakens deterrence.
GS1 youth · GS3 internal security
Unemployed youth in border districts become recruits for gangs, making jobs a security issue.
Crime money in politics: the Gurdaspur MP warns of extortion and drug money entering elections through gangsters' relatives and has sought ED and Income Tax probes.
GS2 · Criminalisation of politics
Crime money entering elections threatens the integrity of democracy in border states.
Beyond policing: police offer rewards for information, and a senior officer suggests reserving 1–2% of vacancies in the Army, police and central forces for border youth.
GS3 · Border area development
Employment and community trust are as vital to border security as policing.
keywords: Criminal gangs and terror networks working together
The crime–terror nexus in Punjab blurs the line between gang violence and terrorism.
A hostile state acting through local criminals
Pakistan-backed gangs show proxy violence through local criminals.
Gang leaders directing operations from abroad
Diaspora-based handlers make Punjab's gang problem transnational.
Quick bail weakening the fear of punishment
A deterrence deficit lets hired shooters return to crime within months.
Crime money and criminals entering the electoral process
Gang money in elections deepens the criminalisation of politics.
Earning local trust to deny support to criminals and militants
Jobs and trust deny gangs local support, the core of winning hearts and minds.
examples: A senior officer proposes 1–2% of Army, police and central force vacancies for youth from border areas
Reserving security-force jobs for border youth turns potential gang recruits into stakeholders in security.
Exposed police posts in border districts
Posts with no boundary walls and few personnel face grenade and gun attacks
Punjab's exposed border posts show why border management needs infrastructure, not just manpower.
Officers say young people with time on their hands turn to gangs
In Punjab's border districts, unemployment pushes youth into gangs, showing joblessness as a security risk.
Gangs reportedly backed by the ISI; a Pakistan-based gangster is a growing name in cross-border narco-terror
Pakistan's backing of gangs in Punjab shows proxy war as a continuing hurdle in India–Pakistan relations.
10–15 gangs run by leaders based in the US, UK, Canada and other countries
Gang networks run from abroad show the misuse of diaspora networks and the need for cooperation with host countries.
pyqs: Linkages between terrorists and organised crime: Punjab's ISI-backed gangs are the live case.
External state and non-state actors: Pakistan-backed gangs and handlers abroad.
Denying local support in border areas: jobs and trust for border youth.

trend.t: Border and security questions moved from managing local perception in border areas (2020) to the challenges of external state and non-state actors (2021) and the crime–terror nexus (2022), and then to border-wide challenges with China and Pakistan (2024) and development-led approaches such as BADP in Ladakh (2026).
trend.watch: Security with a people angle recurs: winning local support (2020) and border area development (2026). The crime–terror nexus and external actors are must-study areas.
focus: External state and non-state actors, including diaspora-based handlers
Border area development and youth employment
Criminalisation of politics in border states

potential: "Punjab's border districts face a security challenge rooted as much in youth unemployment as in cross-border networks." Examine, and suggest a holistic strategy. (15 marks)
Discuss how diaspora-based criminal networks pose a threat to India's internal security. What measures are needed? (10 marks)
Explain the linkages between organised crime and terrorism in India's border states, with examples. (10 marks)

practice.q: Discuss how diaspora-based criminal networks pose a threat to India's internal security. What measures are needed?
parts: Introduction: the Punjab example in one line

answer.t: Punjab Police estimate 10–15 gangs operate in the state with leaders based in the US, UK, Canada and other countries.

pts.t: Leaders abroad direct killings and extortion beyond the reach of Indian law.
pts.ex: Attacks on police and sarpanchs in Punjab's border districts.

pts.t: Gangs merge with terror and narco networks backed by hostile states.
Handlers hire local youth cheaply through social media.
Extortion and drug money flows across borders.
Host countries' reluctance to act strains bilateral ties.
Crime money enters elections through gangsters' relatives.
Extradition treaties, mutual legal assistance and intelligence sharing with host countries.
Financial investigation of extortion and drug proceeds.
Employment schemes and recruitment quotas to deny gangs recruits.

answer.t: A transnational threat needs a transnational response, paired with jobs and trust at home.

title: On theatre commands, let's finish arguing, reach a settlement, before next crisis comes
where: The Ideas Page, page 11 (Arun Prakash, former Navy chief)
syllabus: GS3 › Security forces and agencies and their mandate; Security challenges · GS4 › Leadership; Ethical dilemmas in government institutions
summary: Former Navy chief Arun Prakash says seven years after the CDS was told to create theatre commands, inter-service turf wars stall them; politicians must force a settlement before the next crisis.
evolution: After Kargil, the review committee and Group of Ministers flag the need for jointness; Andaman and Nicobar Command becomes India's only tri-service theatre command (2001).
First Chief of Defence Staff and Department of Military Affairs; theatre commands part of the mandate.
Inter-Services Organisations (Command, Control and Discipline) Act gives joint commanders disciplinary powers over all services.
Theatre commands still not created; the Ideas Page calls it a 'seven-year stasis'.
ideas: Turf over principle: each service's worry is legitimate (Army: air support; IAF: scarce squadrons; Navy: a continental mindset starving it), but the debate has become a turf quarrel.
GS3 · Defence reforms
Theatre commands are stalled less by principle than by inter-service turf: the Army fears losing air support, the IAF its scarce squadrons, the Navy its budget.
17 single-service commands with mismatched boundaries would be caught flat-footed in fast, AI-guided war; one theatre commander should own the forces and the fight.
GS3 · Jointness / modern warfare
India's 17 geographically dispersed single-service commands cannot coordinate fast enough for AI-guided, algorithmic warfare.
Theatreisation keeps 'centralised control, decentralised execution' of air power; only the controller changes, advised by an IAF component commander.
GS3 · Air power debate
Theatre commands need not break the IAF's doctrine: air power stays centrally controlled, but by the theatre commander.
Learn from others: the US settled roles under political authority (Key West, 1948) and achieved jointness through law (Goldwater-Nichols, 1986).
GS3 · Global practice
As the US showed with Key West and Goldwater-Nichols, jointness needs political will and law, not just service consensus.
Politicians must broker the deal: civil and political authority should negotiate roles, win the confidence of all three services and set a deadline, as US leaders did at Key West.
GS3 · Civil-military relations
Political leadership must negotiate with all three services and win their confidence, settling roles by agreement as the US did at Key West (1948).
Leadership is the missing link: bold chiefs, a CDS as honest broker, and a government with a formal national security strategy.
GS3 security · GS4 leadership
Jointness needs bold service chiefs, a CDS who can broker and persuade, and a formal national security strategy.
keywords: One commander controlling all forces in a geographic theatre
Theatre commands would replace 17 single-service commands with integrated, theatre-wise command.
The services planning and fighting as one
Jointness, not more hardware, is the force multiplier India's military lacks.
Principal military adviser; heads the Department of Military Affairs
The CDS must act as an 'honest broker-cum-persuader' among the services.
Inter-service rivalry over roles and resources
The theatre debate has become a turf war 'garbed in the language of high principles'.
IAF doctrine for scarce air assets
Theatreisation preserves 'centralised control, decentralised execution' of air power.
Fast, data-driven warfare leaving no time for coordination across commands
AI-guided warfare will not allow time to coordinate across arbitrary command boundaries.
US settlement of service roles; US law that enforced jointness
The US needed Key West and, four decades later, Goldwater-Nichols to achieve true jointness.
A formal document setting security goals and roles
India still lacks a formal national security strategy to anchor military reform.
Service roles should be settled by agreement under civilian political authority.
Reform needs leaders willing to break old shibboleths.
data: Geographically dispersed single-service military commands in India
India's 17 single-service commands have boundaries that do not match each other.
Since the CDS was directed to create theatre commands
Seven years after the CDS was created, theatre commands remain on paper.
examples: Without a traditional navy, Ukraine crippled Russia's Black Sea Fleet and sank its flagship
Ukraine sank the cruiser Moskva without a traditional navy, showing how drones and missiles change war.
With its air force decimated, Iran attacked 14 US bases in West Asia and contested the Persian Gulf
Iran, its air force decimated, still struck 14 US bases with missiles and drones.
A non-pilot engineer heads the RAF (2023) and becomes CDS (2025); a Royal Marine heads the Royal Navy
Britain's choice of a non-pilot as RAF chief and then CDS shows open-minded, decisive leadership.
Army gave up fixed-wing aircraft for combat helicopters by negotiated agreement
In 1966 the US Army and Air Force swapped roles by agreement, a model for settling turf disputes.
pyqs: Role of security forces on the borders: theatre commands would integrate them under one commander per front.
A two-front border with China and Pakistan is the strongest case for theatre commands.
Weapon acquisitions must fit a joint structure; India is 'on the verge of major weapon acquisition commitments'.
Defence reform covers both structure (theatre commands) and industry (FDI, self-reliance).

trend.t: UPSC has asked defence mainly through equipment and industry (FDI in defence 2014, Indo-US vs Indo-Russian deals 2020, S-400 2021) and through the role of security forces on the borders (2020, 2024). Structural military reform, the CDS and theatre commands, has not yet been asked directly.
trend.watch: Borders and security forces come up almost every year, yet military reform is unasked. With the CDS seven years old and theatre commands pending, defence reform is a must-prepare topic for GS3.
focus: Theatre commands, the CDS and jointness
Changing nature of warfare: drones, missiles, AI, and what it means for India
Self-reliance in defence (Atmanirbhar Bharat) and acquisitions
A national security strategy and civil-military relations

potential: Theatre commands are essential for jointness in India's armed forces, yet progress remains slow. Discuss the need for theatre commands and the challenges in establishing them. (15 marks)
Discuss the role of the Chief of Defence Staff in promoting jointness among the armed forces. (10 marks)
The changing nature of warfare, with drones, missiles and AI, demands changes in India's military structure. Examine. (15 marks)
Does India need a formal national security strategy? Discuss. (10 marks)

practice.q: Theatre commands are essential for jointness in India's armed forces, yet progress remains slow. Discuss the need for theatre commands and the challenges in establishing them.
parts: Introduction: CDS mandate and the delay (one line, with facts)
Way forward (15 marks, so a separate part)

answer.t: Seven years after the first CDS (January 2020) was tasked with theatreisation, India still runs 17 single-service commands, with only the Andaman and Nicobar Command (2001) truly tri-service.

pts.t: A conflict with China or Pakistan would cut across several single-service commands at once.
pts.ex: Western and northern fronts, plus the sea.

pts.t: AI-guided, algorithmic warfare leaves no time to coordinate across mismatched boundaries.
Pooling aircraft, ships and logistics avoids duplication.
pts.ex: IAF well below its sanctioned 42 squadrons.

pts.t: One commander with authority and forces makes faster, clearer decisions.
Joint requirements prevent each service buying for itself.
pts.ex: India is on the verge of major weapon purchases.

pts.t: Major militaries fight jointly by law.
Each service fears losing control of assets and roles.
pts.ex: Army: air support; IAF: squadrons; Navy: budget.

pts.t: The IAF argues that dividing scarce assets breaks 'centralised control, decentralised execution'.
The Navy fears a land-focused structure will starve maritime needs.
Much of the defence budget goes to salaries and pensions, leaving little for restructuring.
Without stated goals, roles of each service stay contested.
Reform needs politicians to arbitrate, as US leaders did at Key West.
Settle roles under civilian authority, with a deadline.
Define threats, theatres and service roles.
Build on the Inter-Services Organisations Act, 2023 with a Goldwater-Nichols-style law.
Central control of air assets by the theatre commander, advised by an IAF component commander.
Make joint service a requirement for promotion.
Build drones, missiles and AI into joint doctrine.

answer.t: The next crisis will not wait for the services to finish arguing; theatre commands must come through political will, law and a clear strategy.

title: China says it is strictly abiding by pacts with India amid LAC face-offs in Arunachal
syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood · GS3 › Security challenges in border areas
context: Days after the ITBP chief spoke of face-offs at several locations in Arunachal Pradesh, China said it strictly abides by agreements and conducts normal patrols. India's MEA said friction occurs when Chinese forces depart from established patrolling patterns in border pockets.
ideas: Normalisation since Galwan is real but fragile: friction on the ground keeps returning.
GS2 · India–China
Six years after Galwan, India–China normalisation remains fragile as face-offs recur along the LAC.
Dialogue at many levels (Corps Commander, diplomatic, leaders) keeps small incidents from escalating.
GS2/GS3 · Border management
Multi-level talks, from Corps Commanders to leaders, keep LAC incidents from escalating.
keywords: A persistent trust deficit outlasts every India–China border agreement.
The three stages of easing a military stand-off
Disengagement must be followed by de-escalation and de-induction for real peace on the LAC.
Steps that reduce the risk of miscalculation
Confidence-building measures reduce the risk of 'misunderstanding and miscalculation' on the LAC.
Ties must rest on the 'three mutuals': mutual respect, sensitivity and interest.
examples: Deadly clash followed by a stand-off of over four years
The 2020 Galwan clash was followed by a military stand-off of over four years.
pyqs: Recurring face-offs in Arunachal show why border infrastructure and the ITBP's role on the China border matter.
Border management needs mechanisms like Corps Commander talks to avoid 'misunderstanding and miscalculation'.
summary: Fresh face-offs in Arunachal Pradesh: China says it follows the border pacts; India says friction comes when Chinese patrols depart from agreed patterns.
evolution: Deadly Galwan clashes, followed by a military face-off that lasted over four years.
Both sides took measures to rebuild relations.
Corps Commander talks at the Wacha-Damai border meeting point.
Modi and Xi met at the BRICS summit in New Delhi; Modi stressed the 'three mutuals'.
